excerpt: Kremlinology for LLM Infrastructure Kremlinology was the art of speculating about the inner workings of the Soviet central command headquartered in the Kremlin. Because it was a highly closed and secretive group, its thinking mostly had to be inferred indirectly, filling in the gaps from the downstream results of visible policy actions. When it comes to inference providers in our modern day and age, we find ourselves similarly situated in some ways. We are told that a model is being served at an endpoint, and we can call it and get responses back, but in many ways the inner workings remain a mystery. What hardware is it running on? What optimizations or approximations are being used? In some cases, is a different model being used entirely? Is someone else actually the one serving it? There are ways and means of figuring this out, but to my knowledge they haven't been extensively explored or used in public. For open-weight models, at least, we have a good idea of what serving would or should look like, including under various optimizations. For closed models, there are a fair number of educated guesses we can make about what is going on. We have a number of signals to work with: time to first token (TTFT), fairly detailed inter-token latency (ITL) from streaming responses, logprobs in some cases, API design, cache hits and misses, and usage counters. I looked at these signals on a bunch of inference providers, mostly serving open-weight models on OpenRouter. I used synthetic prompts and public datasets, and for tens of dollars of API spend and lots of analysis was able to learn a lot about how the models were served: which providers are serving the same thing, what you learn from API bugs, what generation speed tells you about speculative decoding, and so on.
